title: Logging Framework
summary: A deceptively deep 'simple' prompt: levels, sinks, and formatting look trivial until the interviewer asks what happens when a sink is slow — then it's an async-delivery design problem.

slides.markdown:
"Design a logging framework" reads like a warm-up question, and answering "just call `print()` with a timestamp" fails it immediately — real logging frameworks need levels, multiple destinations, formatting, and, once probed, a way to avoid blocking the application when a destination is slow.

The interview arc mirrors most real systems: it starts simple (levels and sinks), then the interviewer pulls one thread — "what if writing to disk takes 50ms and you log 10,000 times a second?" — and the whole design has to grow an async delivery pipeline without changing the caller's experience.

slides.sectionTitle: Requirements: levels, destinations, formatting, low overhead
slides.markdown:
The core contract: support **log levels** (DEBUG through ERROR, at minimum), write to **multiple destinations** at once (console, file, a cloud log service), apply consistent **formatting**, and impose **minimal performance overhead** on the code that calls `logger.info(...)` — a hot request path shouldn't stall on logging.

**Non-goals** worth stating up front: this is a client-side logging library, not a full log-aggregation backend — no search, no indexing, no cross-service correlation. Naming that boundary early keeps the design focused on the actual LLD, not a distributed-systems tangent.

slides.sectionTitle: Core entities: Logger, LogLevel, LogRecord, Appender, Formatter
slides.markdown:
Five classes carry the whole design. A **`Logger`** is the entry point callers use (`logger.info("msg")`). **`LogLevel`** is an ordered enum (DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR) used to filter what actually gets emitted. A **`LogRecord`** is the immutable data produced by one log call — message, level, timestamp, caller context. An **`Appender`** (also called a sink) is a destination — console, file, network — that knows how to write a record out. A **`Formatter`** turns a `LogRecord` into the string or structure an `Appender` actually writes.

Keeping these separate is what makes the rest of the design extensible: a `Logger` never talks to a file or a socket directly, it only ever talks to `Appender` and `Formatter` interfaces.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a log call flowing through filter, format, and fan-out
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: a horizontal pipeline — a "logger.info() call" box, arrow into a "level check" diamond, arrow (if passed) into a "Formatter" box, then fanning out with three arrows into three "Appender" boxes labelled Console, File, Cloud; a fourth arrow from the level-check diamond looping back labelled "dropped" for records that fail the filter >>>

One log call becomes: a level check that can drop the record entirely before any work happens, then one formatting pass, then a fan-out to every registered appender. Formatting happens once and is reused by all appenders — it isn't repeated per destination.

This is the shape every later addition builds on: a new destination is a new box on the fan-out side, never a change to the pipeline itself.

slides.sectionTitle: Chain of Responsibility for level filtering
slides.markdown:
A clean way to implement the level check is the **Chain of Responsibility** pattern: a chain of handlers — DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR — where each handler decides whether to pass a record along based on the configured minimum level, rather than one big if/elif ladder inside `Logger`.

Concretely, each handler wraps the next one; if the logger's configured level is INFO, the DEBUG handler is skipped (or the chain simply starts at INFO). The benefit isn't performance — a single comparison would be just as fast — it's that adding a new level, or per-handler side effects (like counting how many WARN-and-above records fired), doesn't require touching `Logger` at all, only the chain.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: adding a new appender without touching Logger
Should Logger be a Singleton? The usual instinct vs the real trade-off
slides.markdown:
The instinctive answer is yes — there should be "one logger" the whole app shares, so a Singleton feels natural. But a single global `Logger` makes two things harder: **per-module level overrides** (you often want DEBUG logs from one noisy module without turning them on everywhere), and **testing** (a Singleton's global state leaks between test cases unless carefully reset).

Most real frameworks — Log4j, Python's `logging`, SLF4J — instead use a **registry of loggers keyed by name**, typically the class or module name (`getLogger("payments.service")`). Each named logger can have its own level and appenders, while still sharing the underlying appender/formatter machinery. It looks like a Singleton from the call site (`getLogger(name)` always returns the same instance for that name) but isn't a single global object.

slides.sectionTitle: The hard part: synchronous logging blocks the caller
slides.markdown:
Every appender call in the pipeline so far runs **on the caller's thread**. A console write is fast, but a file write can hit disk latency, and a cloud appender makes a network call — both can take milliseconds to seconds under load, and that cost lands directly on whatever code called `logger.info()`, even a hot request path.

**Async logging** fixes throughput by having the caller hand off the `LogRecord` and return immediately, with a separate thread doing the actual, slower write. But this trades one problem for another: what happens when producers (callers logging) create records faster than the writer thread can drain them? That queue-growth problem is the real design question async logging introduces, and it's what the next few slides solve.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: an async Logger backed by a bounded queue and writer thread
Diagram: producer threads, a bounded queue, one writer thread
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: multiple "producer thread" boxes on the left each with an arrow labelled "enqueue LogRecord" into a single "bounded queue" box in the middle, annotated with a callout "full policy: block / drop / discard-oldest"; one arrow from the queue into a single "writer thread" box on the right, which fans out into the appenders >>>

Many producers, one consumer, and a queue in between that has to have an explicit **full policy** — what happens when producers outrun the writer and the bounded queue fills up. Leaving this undefined is the single most common gap in an async-logging design.

The three standard choices: **block** the producer until space frees up (safest, but reintroduces the latency async was meant to remove), **drop** the new record (loses data, protects latency), or **discard-oldest** (evicts the oldest queued record to make room for the newest, favoring recency).

Neither mode is strictly better — they trade latency for durability guarantees.

| | Synchronous | Asynchronous |
|---|---|---|
| Caller latency | Coupled to I/O (disk/network) per call | Decoupled — enqueue is O(1) |
| Ordering | Guaranteed per-thread | Guaranteed within the queue, but a burst can reorder relative to real time under a full-policy drop |
| Durability on crash | Every logged record is written before the call returns | Queued-but-undrained records can be lost unless flushed on shutdown |
| Throughput ceiling | Limited by the slowest appender | Limited by the writer thread and queue capacity, not caller speed |

**How to decide:** default to async for anything on a request's hot path; keep synchronous logging only where a record must be durable the instant the call returns — e.g. an audit log for a financial transaction, where losing the tail on crash is unacceptable.

slides.sectionTitle: Backpressure under high volume, deep-dive: sampling and level elevation
slides.markdown:
A bounded queue's full-policy is a blunt, last-resort mitigation. Two proactive strategies reduce how often you hit it. **Sampling** logs only 1-in-N DEBUG (or even INFO) records during normal operation — you keep a statistically useful sample without paying for every single one. **Level elevation under load** temporarily raises the effective minimum level (suppressing DEBUG/INFO) when the queue depth crosses a threshold, automatically shedding low-value volume exactly when the system is under the most pressure.

Both trade completeness for sustainability: you accept losing some low-priority records on purpose, in exchange for never losing high-priority ones (WARN/ERROR) to a full queue.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a logging call that throws and crashes the caller
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Logging is a side effect, so if the formatter or an appender has a bug, it's fine for the exception to propagate — it'll show up in the logs."

**Why it's wrong:** an exception from *inside* the logging call — a formatter bug on unexpected input, a full disk on a file appender — propagates up into the caller's business logic. A payment-processing function that logs a transaction and then crashes because the logger itself threw has turned an observability feature into an outage cause.

**Correct model:** every appender and formatter call must be wrapped so its own failures are caught and reported (e.g. to a fallback stderr write or a metric), never re-thrown into the caller. Logging must be allowed to fail silently from the caller's point of view — it can never be more fragile than the code it's observing.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: making every appender synchronous by default
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll make the whole `Logger` async, but each individual appender can just write synchronously when the writer thread calls it — that's simpler."

**Why it's wrong:** the writer thread in an async design is a single shared resource. If it calls appenders one after another and one of them — say, a cloud appender hitting a slow network — blocks for seconds, every other appender, and every other log record waiting behind it in the queue, stalls too. One slow sink now throttles logging for the entire application.

**Correct model:** either give each appender (or at least each slow, I/O-bound one) its own dedicated writer thread and queue, or make appenders themselves non-blocking (fire-and-forget with their own internal buffering). A single shared writer thread should never be allowed to wait indefinitely on one destination.
